text: One gram of single-stranded DNA can hold 455 exabytes. That is a ceiling set by the molecule, not by an experiment. Four letters, two bits per nucleotide at maximum, so 455 exabytes is 3.6 × 10²¹ bits — and one gram of single-stranded DNA is about 1.8 × 10²¹ nucleotides. The arithmetic closes: this is the density the molecule allows, not something achieved. What was actually written in 2012 was 5.27 megabits — 660 kilobytes — at 5.5 petabits per cubic millimetre, from off-the-shelf DNA. The distance between that and 455 exabytes is synthesis cost and error rate, not physics. 455 exabytes is 455 million one-terabyte drives. And the figure assumes no error-correction overhead: any real archive carries redundancy and lands well below the ceiling. Source: Church, Gao & Kosuri, Science 337, 1628 (2012) · doi.org/10.1126/science.1226355

🧬 Rare disease exposes a hidden immune flaw Researchers at the Garvan Institute of Medical Research have found that in mevalonate kinase deficiency (MKD), a rare genetic disorder, natural killer cells fail to mature and cannot properly destroy infected cells. When these cells miss their targets, they release large amounts of inflammatory signaling molecules, setting off excessive inflammation. The finding, published in Immunity, challenges roughly 30 years of research focused on macrophages. About half of patients do not respond to existing treatments, and the study points to JAK inhibitors as a possible new option. The result is based on blood samples from patients plus preclinical models; no clinical trial has yet tested the new approach. #immunology #genetics #MKD @science

🛰 Voyager 1 crosses one light-day from Earth A light-day is 25.902 billion km — how far light travels in 24 hours. According to JPL Horizons, on 18 November 2026 the probe sits 173.14 AU from Earth (25.901 billion km), with a radio signal taking 23 h 59 min to reach us. It passes the full 24-hour mark on 19 November, around 03:00 UTC. Launched on 5 September 1977, it has flown for almost 49 years. Its speed relative to the Sun is 16.9 km/s, about 3.6 AU per year. The inner edge of the Oort cloud is roughly 300 years away, around 2326; getting out of the cloud will take some 30,000 years. The probe will not leave the galaxy, though: the Oort cloud is still part of the Solar System, and "exit" means only that it clears the outer boundary. #Voyager #space #astronomy @science

💧 New material turns water vapor into an ally for carbon capture Chemists at Oregon State University have created a metal-organic framework called BVR-X that can pull carbon dioxide from wet industrial emissions, where moisture normally undermines capture. Its internal structure keeps water and CO2 in separate regions of the pores, so water no longer blocks the spaces needed for adsorption. A patent application has been filed, and the work is published in Angewandte Chemie. The material works under conditions closer to real industrial flue gas, where water vapor is abundant, and industry accounts for 30% of US greenhouse gas emissions. In the US, that 30% figure comes from the Environmental Protection Agency. #CarbonCapture #MOFs #GreenhouseGases @science

159 correct answers out of 160: South Korean exam candidate caught using a setup involving a camera, AI, and an earpiece 34-year-old Han Won-seok topped the list of candidates for the first stage of the tax consultant examination, making only a single error. Following a public outcry, he contacted the authorities through his lawyer and confessed to cheating. According to him, an ultra-miniature camera captured the exam questions and transmitted them to an AI system, which generated the solutions. He then received the answers via a smartphone and a concealed earpiece. Han admitted to employing this scheme during both stages of the tax consultant examination, as well as during the first stage of the examination for certified public accountants. https://x.com/shanyanggm/status/2122663158796185615

🌊 SCIENTISTS FOUND 245 ANIMALS LIVING INSIDE A SINGLE ROCK — 5,000 METERS BELOW THE OCEAN. And these tiny ecosystems may take millions of years to develop. Researchers from the University of Bremen examined 244 polymetallic nodules — metal-rich rocks scattered across the Pacific seafloor. Inside their microscopic cracks, they discovered 4,139 animals , including one rock sheltering an astonishing 245 individuals. Even more surprising, these tiny creatures formed distinct communities unlike those living in the surrounding mud. Some of these habitats were remarkably similar across locations separated by 1,000 kilometers. Why does this matter? The nodules contain valuable nickel, cobalt and copper — exactly the metals targeted by deep-sea mining. Removing them could destroy unique ecosystems that cannot regenerate on human timescales. The study documents previously overlooked biodiversity, although scientists still don’t know whether some species exist exclusively inside these rocks. We may be preparing to mine ecosystems we have barely begun to discover. #Science #Ocean #MarineBiology #Discovery #Biodiversity https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-76737-w

🤖 Anthropic researcher: superintelligence by late 2027, permanent unemployment for most Tao Lin of Anthropic gave a one-hour interview to Palisade Research with forecasts the company has not endorsed: his personal view. Timeline. "Broad superintelligence" in about 1.3 years — late 2027: an AI as good as the best expert in almost any field. Jobs. "Pretty much all humans will become permanently unemployable and live on benefits." Between an AI that could replace anyone and real replacement sits a gap: robots, and factories to build them. Risk. He puts the chance that AI eventually "removes humanity from the equation" at about 20%, a power grab below 50%. No sci-fi needed: people delegate more, understand less, lose the ability to steer. Slowing research buys only a year or two if only cautious labs slow down. Caveat: one person's forecast, not the company's position; the dates are unverifiable. #AI #Anthropic @science

🔭 Hera reveals the unseen side of the asteroid NASA hit ESA's Hera spacecraft has sent back its first close-up image of the Didymos system, the site of NASA's 2022 DART impact experiment. The image shows the larger asteroid Didymos from a side never seen in such detail, featuring boulders, craters, and puzzling groove-like patterns. Scientists now want to know whether debris from the collision on Dimorphos traveled the roughly 1 km gap and reshaped its neighbor's surface. The 580 kg DART spacecraft struck Dimorphos at about 6.1 km/s, cutting its orbit around Didymos short by roughly 33 minutes, far more than expected. The image was taken from 60 km away in black and white, so surface colors remain unknown. #asteroids #space #Hera @science
